blocks.text: Now, lest anyone object, on the authority of both Kimchis, that the Arabs' قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud is the tortoise, I say that they are gravely mistaken on this point. For in Arabic the tortoise is not called kunphud but سلخفاة [sulaḥfāh] sulachpha, or سلخفية [sulaḥfiya] sulachphia, as if you were to say hiding in a shell or husk: for خفا [khafā] chapha means to hide, and سلخ [salkh] silch, or sulch, is φολὶς [pholis], a covering, properly of a serpent, but also of a tortoise; just as γῆρας [gēras], a word most use for the leberis, or slough of a serpent, but some also for χελωνίω [chelōniō], as Aelian, History book 2, ch. 37, and Suidas under Φολίδωτον [Pholidōton]. But that قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud is the hedgehog no one will deny who has read Damiri, where قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud is surnamed ابو الشوك [abū al-shawk] abussuchi, that is, father of thorns; and انقد [anqad] ankado, that is, the stripper of bark; and ابو سفين [abū safīn] abusaphin, that is, the father who scrapes or polishes, because garments are polished with its [col. 1038] skin; and العساعس [al-ʿasāʿis] alasaiso, because it roams at night. For that is properly عس [ʿassa] assa, as also سري [sarā] sara; hence the proverb in use among them, اسري من قنفذ [asrā min qunfudh], More night-roaming than the kunphud. In the same place you may find many things pertaining to its description, among which these are remarkable: القنفذ ان جاع صعد الكرم منكسا فيقطع العناقيد ويرمي بها ثم ينزل فياكل منها ما اطاق واذا كان له فراخ تمرغ في العناقيد لتشتبك في شوكه ويذهب به الي فراخه وهو لا يظهر الا ليلا وهو مولع باكل الافاع [II, 457] ولا يتالم لها وانا لذعته الحية اكل الصعتر البري فيبري وله خمسة اسنان في فيه والبرية منها تسفد قايمة وظهر الذكر لاصق بظهر الانثي [al-qunfudh in jāʿa ṣaʿida al-karm munakkasan fa-yaqṭaʿu al-ʿanāqīd wa-yarmī bihā thumma yanzilu fa-yaʾkulu minhā mā aṭāqa wa-idhā kāna lahu firākh tamarragha fī al-ʿanāqīd li-tashtabika fī shawkihi wa-yadhhabu bihi ilā firākhihi wa-huwa lā yaẓharu illā laylan wa-huwa mūlaʿ bi-akl al-afāʿ wa-lā yataʾallamu lahā wa-anā ladhaʿathu al-ḥayya akala al-ṣaʿtar al-barrī fa-yabraʾ wa-lahu khamsat asnān fī fīhi wa-al-barriyya minhā tusfadu qāʾima wa-ẓahr al-dhakar lāṣiq bi-ẓahr al-unthā] Alkunphud, when it is hungry, climbs a vine upside down and plucks off the clusters, which it throws down. Then, coming down from there, it eats of them as much as it can. If it has young, it rolls about in the clusters so that they become entangled in its spines, and with them it hurries to its young. It does not appear except at night. It has a wonderful appetite for eating vipers, and is not harmed by them. When bitten by a serpent, it is healed by eating wild marjoram. It has five teeth in its mouth. The land kunphud copulates upright, so that the back of the male clings to the back of the female. Everyone sees that these things pertain to the hedgehog, although among them there are some that you would seek in vain in the Greeks. Now, if we consult the physicians, say Avicenna, Ibn al-Baitar and that same Damiri mentioned above, we shall find not only that they attribute to the kunphud the same virtues that the Greek writers attribute to the ἐχίνῳ [echinō], but also that, in rendering the passages of Dioscorides and Galen on the land and sea hedgehog, they consistently call the former القنفذ البري [al-qunfudh al-barrī] alkunphud albarri, or land hedgehog, the latter القنفذ البحري [al-qunfudh al-baḥrī] alkunphud albahari, or sea hedgehog. Not to mention that the translators of the Prophets, who made the Arabic version from the Greek, everywhere rendered the Greek ἐχίνους [echinous] by القنافذ [al-qanāfidh] alkanaphido, which is the plural of kunphud. For examples see Esa. XIV, 23. and XXXIV, 11. and Sophon. II, 14. Accordingly, among the Hebrews, R. Nathan, far more learned in Arabic than Kimchi, readily acknowledges that قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud is the hedgehog. Further, that the Hebrews' קפוד kippod, the Chaldeans' קופד kuphad, and the Arabs' قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud are the same animal, anyone who has some taste of these languages will at once recognize. The long vowel in קופד kuphad makes up for the lack of the Daghesh point found in קפוד kippod. And that very Daghesh is replaced by the letter Nun, which shows itself in the Arabic قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud, as also in [col. 1039] the Ethiopic ቀንፈዝ፡ konphoz of the same meaning. Thus חטה chitta, that is, wheat, stands for חנטה chinta, as the Arabs write it. The wood of which the ark of the testimony was made is called שטה sitta, for שנטה sinta; as in Arabic سنط [sanṭ] sent. The spider is עכביש accabis, for ancabis; as in Arabic عنكبوث [ʿankabūth] ancabuths. And עז ez, that is, goat, plural עזים izzim, is in Arabic عنز [ʿanz] enz. This is to be noted here against those who trace the word קפוד kippod to the root קפד kaphad, so that it would signify an animal endowed with some peculiar power of cutting. But the true root is not קפד kaphad, but the unused קנפד kanphad; unless someone thinks that the word is a compound, with the gutturals elided (as happens), of קנה kana, which is a dart, and אפד aphad, which is to clothe, because this animal is clothed and fenced about with spines and prickles as with darts. Or, if you prefer that the Nun in قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud is epenthetic, even the root קפד kaphad has certain meanings which [II, 458] you could refer here. As when קפדן kaphdan is used of a harsh and irascible man. In this sense, in Sanhedrin, chapter 11, the prophet Elijah is said to have been קפדן. And in the tractate On the Sabbath, ch. 2, fol. 30b: לעולם יהא אדם ענותן כהלל ואל יהא קפדן כשמאי, Let a man always be gentle like Hillel, and not kaphdan (or irascible) like Shammai. Because, as the Pomarius says, a harsh and irascible man is כמו הקפוד עם קוצים, like a hedgehog with spines. So these Greek proverbs, Ἐχῖνου τραχύτερος [Echinou trachyteros] and Ἅπας ἐχῖνος τραχὺς [Hapas echinos trachys], signify a morose and intractable man. To the same point belongs the fact that קפד kaphad, or הקפיד hikphid, means to be attentive and anxious, and הקפדה hakkephada means attention and anxiety; because, as is in the Pomarius, when the hedgehog קורץ כל גופו, covers its whole body with spines, its face hiding between its feet, and raises its prickles, with which it defends itself as with a shield and wounds those who wish to lay violent hands on it, פעולת הזאת היא השגחה והרגשה נמרצת, this action is one of providence and the keenest attention. Moreover, ܩܦܕ for the Syrians is to shudder, or to bristle, as when the hairs stand on end from fear, as in hedgehogs. So in the Syriac Psalm 119, verse 120: ܩܦܕ ܒܣܪܝ ܡܢ ܕܚܠܬܟ, My flesh shuddered for fear of you, that is, the hairs of my flesh stood on end, as is found in Iob. IV, 15. In French you would say herisser by the same metaphor. For herisser, that is, ὀρθοτριχεῖν [orthotrichein], to bristle, and herisson are cognates.
